{"self_assessment": "**Impact**
I picked the animal and drew the plan on the pad: a side-view fish, nose left, with a wide forked tail. I chose it because the outline alone says fish. The chain was fully connected from the start, with nothing left standing apart at the last check. I can't say yet whether the judge recognized it. The tail came out a bit rounder and looser than the crisp fork I sketched, and I never added an eye or fins. We used only about 137 of 250 dominoes, so we left some detail on the table.

**Execution**
I laid the start line and nose, then the top tail prong when I saw it was still empty. I also checked the joint and the chain for gaps. The sketch-then-trace approach kept the shape consistent and let everyone build in parallel. I kept my own hands away from the body once it was connected, to avoid bumps. One weakness is that I didn't push for the extra detail while there was time and material.

**Collaboration**
I gave each person a stroke by number. When Priya's prong was lagging, I covered it so she could move to the belly. I let Tom lift the stray dominoes after confirming they weren't on the pad, and I told him to leave the dark line alone. Maya, Tom and Priya each closed gaps and cleaned up strays. I tried to avoid duplicate work and bumps by keeping people apart.

**Leadership**
I set the plan in the first minute, assigned the strokes, and reassigned people when the belly fell behind. I called the hands-off point once the chain was clean. My style is directive, and it worked here because the team agreed quickly. In hindsight I could have used the idle last minutes, when we all stood by, to add the eye or a fin before calling hands-off."}
